source_text: f De generationibus si cetera delictorum recogitemus, inprimis cupiditatem radicem omnium malorum, qua quidam inretiti circa fidem naufragium sunt passi, cum bis et idololatria ab eodem apostolo dicta sit cupiditas, tum mendacium cupiditatis ministrum — taceo de periurio, quando ne iurare quidem liceat — negotiatio seruo dei apta est? ceterum si cupiditas abscedat, quae est causa adquirendi? cessante causa adquirendi non erit necessitas negotiandi. sit nunc aliqua iustitia quaestus secura de cupiditatis et mendacii obseruatione, in crimen offendere idololatriae eam opinor, quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet, quae omne daemonium saginat. sane non illa principalis idololatria? uiderint, si eaedem merces, tura dico et cetera peregrinitatis ad sacrificium idolorum etiam hominibus ad pigmenta medicinalia, nobis quoque insuper ad solacia sepulturae usui sunt. certe cum pompae, cum sacerdotia, cum sacrificia idolorum de periculis, de damnis, de incommodis, de cogitationibus, de discursibus negotiationibusue instruuntur, quid aliud quam procurator idolorum demonstraris ? nemo contendat posse hoc modo omnibus negotiationibus controuersiam fieri. grauiora delicta quaeque pro magnitudine periculi diligentiam extendunt obseruationis, ut non ab his tantum abscedamus, sed et ab iis per quae fiunt. licet enim ab aliis fiat, non interest, si per me. in nullo necessarius esse debeo alii, cum facit quod mihi non licet. ex hoc, quod uetor facere, intellegere debeo curandum mihi esse, ne fiat per me. denique in alia causa non leuioris reatus praeiudicium istud obseruo. nam quod mihi de stupro interdictum sit, aliis ad eam rem nihil aut operae aut conscientiae exhibeo. nam quod ipsam carnem meam a lupanaribus segregaui, agnosco me neque lenocinium neque id genus lucrum alterius causa exercere posse. sic et homicidii interdictio ostendit mihi lanistam quoque ab ecclesia arceri: nec per se non faciet quod faciendum alio subministrat. ecce magis proximum praeiudicium. si publicarum uictimarum redemptor ad fidem accedat, permittes ei in eo negotio permanere? aut si iam fidelis id agere susceperit, retinendum in ecclesia putabis? non opinor, nisi si quis et de turario dissimulabit. scilicet ad alios peruenit procuratio sanguinis, ad alios odorum. si, antequam idola in saeculo essent, his mercibus adhuc informis idololatria transigebatur, si et nunc fere sine idolo opus idololatriae incendiis odorum perpetratur, ecquid maioris operae et erga daemonia turarius? nam facilius sine idolo idololatria, quam sine turarii merce. ipsius fidei conscientiam perrogemus. quo ore Christianus turarius, si per templa transibit, quo ore fumantes aras despuet et exsufflabit, quibus ipse prospexit? qua constantia exorcizabit alumnos suos, quibus domum suam cellarium praestat? ille quidem si excluserit daemonium, non sibi placeat de fide. neque enim inimicum exclusit. facile debuit de eo impetrare, quem cotidie pascit. nulla igitur ars, nulla professio, nulla negotiatio, quae quid aut instruendis aut formandis idolis administrat, carere poterit titulo idololatriae;
thought_title: Trade that serves idols is idolatry
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christians must avoid every trade that supplies idol worship, now turning from schoolteachers to merchants and dealers in sacrificial goods.
pass_a_gloss: But if we reconsider the other offenses, first of all desire, the root of all evils, by which some, entangled, have suffered shipwreck concerning faith, since desire has been called idolatry by the same apostle, and also lying, the servant of desire — I am silent about perjury, since it is not even permitted to swear — is trade fitting for a servant of God? But if desire departs, what is the cause of acquiring? When the cause of acquiring ceases, there will be no necessity of trading. Let there now be some justice of profit, free from the observance of desire and lying; I think that it offends into the crime of idolatry, which pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols, which fattens every demon. Is that not indeed the principal idolatry? Let them see, if the same goods, I mean frankincense and other foreign things for the sacrifice of idols, are also useful to men for medicinal pigments, and to us moreover for the consolations of burial. Certainly when the processions, when the priesthoods, when the sacrifices of idols are furnished from dangers, from losses, from inconveniences, from plans, from running about and from trading, what else will you be shown to be than a procurer of idols? Let no one contend that in this way a controversy can be made with all trades. The graver offenses each extend the diligence of observance according to the greatness of the danger, so that we should withdraw not only from these things, but also from those things through which they happen. For although it is done by others, it makes no difference, if it is done through me. In nothing ought I to be necessary to another, when he does what is not permitted to me. From this, that I am forbidden to do, I ought to understand that I must take care that it not be done through me. Finally in another case of no lighter guilt I observe this precedent. For since fornication has been forbidden to me, I furnish to others for that matter nothing either of work or of knowledge. For since I have separated my own flesh from brothels, I recognize that I can practice neither pimping nor that kind of profit for another's sake. So also the prohibition of homicide shows me that the trainer of gladiators is also kept away from the church: nor will he fail to do through himself what he supplies for another to do. Behold a nearer precedent. If a buyer of public victims should come to faith, will you permit him to remain in that business? Or if already a believer should undertake to do this, will you think he should be retained in the church? I do not think so, unless someone will also overlook the frankincense dealer. Of course the procurement of blood reaches some, of odors reaches others. If, before idols were in the world, formless idolatry was carried on with these goods, if even now almost without an idol the work of idolatry is accomplished by burnings of odors, is the frankincense dealer of any greater work also toward demons? For idolatry is easier without an idol than without the frankincense dealer's goods. Let us question the conscience of faith itself. With what face will a Christian frankincense dealer, if he passes through temples, with what face will he spit upon and blow upon the smoking altars, for which he himself has provided? With what constancy will he exorcise his own nurslings, to whom he furnishes his house as a storehouse? That man indeed, if he casts out a demon, let him not please himself about faith. For he has not cast out an enemy. He ought easily to have obtained power over him whom he feeds daily. Therefore no art, no profession, no trade, which administers anything either for equipping or for forming idols, will be able to lack the title of idolatry;

choices.english: desire, the root of all evils
choices.why: Keeps the Pauline phrase literal; 'desire' matches the glossary's moral sense of cupiditas as acquisitive craving.
Procurer preserves the legal and moral force of one who supplies what others use for wrongdoing.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for this trade term.
Alumnus means one nourished or reared; 'nurslings' keeps the ironic image of the dealer feeding demons.
Cellarium is a storeroom or pantry; the dealer's house becomes a supply depot for demons.
Exsufflare is the ritual act of blowing away evil; 'blow upon' keeps the physical gesture literal.

bible_refs.note: qua quidam inretiti circa fidem naufragium sunt passi

pass_b_english: Now let us consider the other kinds of wrongdoing that arise from trade. First, desire, the root of all evils, by which some have been entangled and have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith. Since the same apostle calls desire idolatry, and lying is desire's servant—I say nothing of perjury, since we are not even permitted to swear—is trade fitting for a servant of God? If desire departs, what reason is left for acquiring? When the reason for acquiring ceases, there will be no necessity for trading.

But suppose there is some just profit, free from the taint of desire and lying. I maintain that it still offends against idolatry, because it pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols and fattens every demon. Is that not idolatry in its primary form? Let them consider whether the same merchandise—I mean frankincense and other foreign goods used for idol sacrifice—is also useful to people for medicinal ointments, and to us as well for burial comforts. Certainly, when processions, priesthoods, and idol sacrifices are equipped through your dangers, losses, hardships, plans, errands, and trading, what else are you shown to be but a procurer of idols?

Let no one argue that this would make every kind of trade a matter of dispute. The graver the sin, the more diligently we must extend our watchfulness, so that we withdraw not only from the sins themselves but also from the means by which they are committed. Even if the act is done by others, it makes no difference if it is done through me. I must not be necessary to another when he does what is not permitted to me. From the fact that I am forbidden to do something, I should understand that I must take care that it not be done through me.

I observe this principle in another matter of no lighter guilt. Since I am forbidden from fornication, I provide no labor or complicity to others for that purpose. Since I have separated my own flesh from brothels, I recognize that I cannot practice pimping or any profit of that kind for another's sake. Likewise, the prohibition of homicide shows me that a trainer of gladiators is also barred from the church: he does not commit the act himself, but he supplies what another does.

Here is an even closer precedent. If a buyer of public victims comes to the faith, will you permit him to remain in that business? Or if he has already become a believer and undertakes it, will you think he should be retained in the church? I do not think so, unless someone will also overlook the frankincense dealer. Of course, the procurement of blood reaches some, and the procurement of fragrances reaches others.

If, before idols existed in the world, idolatry in its unformed state was carried on by these goods, and if even now the work of idolatry is nearly accomplished without an idol through the burning of fragrances, what greater service does the frankincense dealer render to demons? For idolatry is easier without an idol than without the frankincense dealer's merchandise.

Let us question the conscience of his faith itself. With what face will a Christian frankincense dealer pass through temples? With what face will he spit upon and blow upon the smoking altars for which he himself has provided? With what steadfastness will he exorcise his own nurslings, to whom he offers his house as a storehouse? If he casts out a demon, let him not congratulate himself on his faith. He has not cast out an enemy. He should easily obtain victory over the one he feeds daily.
Therefore no art, no profession, no trade that supplies anything for the equipping or forming of idols will be able to escape the charge of idolatry.

fixed: The source says 'quae ad ipsam idolorum animam et spiritum pertinet' — 'which pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols.' The English 'it touches' is close but 'pertains to' is more accurate to 'pertinet'. The suggested 'nourishes the very life of idolatry' is not supported by the source, which explicitly mentions 'animam et spiritum' of idols. I changed 'touches' to 'pertains to' for accuracy.

The source says 'de incommodis' — 'from inconveniences' or 'from hardships'. The Latin 'incommodis' can mean 'inconveniences' or 'hardships'. The suggested 'hardships' is a reasonable rendering, so I changed it.

last_rejected.ruling: "non sibi placeat de fide" = let him not be pleased with himself regarding his faith; "congratulate himself on his faith" is a valid rendering, not an addition.

polish.changed: Broke the long passage into shorter paragraphs at natural turns of thought, clarified pronoun references (e.g., 'he' as the frankincense dealer), and kept every claim and qualification intact while smoothing the sentence flow for modern readers.
